A tested CLI tool with clear errors and exit codes

scenes.question: An agent may only use the tools `search` and `calculator`. Which structure gives the fastest "is this tool allowed?" check?
scenes.explain: Membership checks on a **set** are fast however many items it holds, and duplicates are impossible.

scenes.question: What does `@dataclass(frozen=True)` add to `UsageRecord`?
options: Fields can't be changed after creation
scenes.explain: Frozen dataclasses raise an error if you assign to a field after creation. Note: a dataclass does **not** validate types; that's why `from_dict` checks them.

scenes.question: In `try / except / else / finally`, which block runs every time?
scenes.explain: `finally` always runs, success or failure, which makes it the place for cleanup.

scenes.question: Why does `fetch_all` use `asyncio.gather`?
options: To download all URLs concurrently, so total time ≈ the slowest one
scenes.explain: `gather` waits for all downloads at once. It saves waiting time; it doesn't add CPU power.

scenes.question: Where should the real API key for your project live?
options: In an environment variable or a git-ignored `.env`
scenes.explain: Secrets live in environment variables (or a `.env` that is in `.gitignore`). `.env.example` holds only fake placeholder values.

captions.text: Welcome back.
The data layer works.
Now we add the report writer, the downloader, and the command line, then run the
finished tool, test it, fix the common errors, and finish the module with a quiz and
a challenge.
Render markdown takes a summary and returns text.
It doesn't print anything, so it's easy to test, and the caller decides where the
text goes.
The report is built as a list of lines, using f-string formats from lesson two.
Colon point one percent shows a percentage, and colon point four f shows four
decimal places.
A Markdown table has one row per model.
Then the top tags, numbered with enumerate, a warning if any model had no price, and
finally join glues everything into one string.
The JSON report builds nested dictionaries in exactly the shape we want, rounding
the floats so the output stays tidy.
A dictionary comprehension builds the per-model section, and a list comprehension
builds the tags.
Sets aren't valid JSON, so the unpriced models become a sorted list.
And json dot dumps turns it all into text.
Fetch one is the async request from lesson five.
Get the URL, raise for status, and parse the JSON.
Each kind of failure becomes one readable toolkit error.
An error status, a network problem like a refused connection, or a body that isn't
JSON.
And the body has to be a list of records.
Fetch all opens one client, gathers every download at the same time, and flattens
the batches into one list, keeping the order of the URLs.
The optional transport parameter is for testing.
It lets tests replace the real network with a fake one.
The standard library's argparse turns command line text into Python values.
It also generates help text and error messages for free.
Sub parsers give us separate commands, like git commit and git push.
Validate takes one file, and type equals Path converts it to a Path object.
Report adds options: a format restricted to two choices, an optional output file,
and a strict flag that is True when present.
Fetch accepts one or more URLs, and requires an output file.
Each command is a function that returns an exit code.
Validate prints every problem and returns one if anything was wrong, so scripts and
CI pipelines can detect failure.
Report loads settings and records.
Warnings go to standard error, so they never mix into a report that's being saved or
piped.
With strict, any invalid record is a failure.
Then we summarise and choose a renderer, Markdown or JSON.
The text is written to a file if out was given, or printed.
Fetch uses asyncio dot run to call our async function from normal code.
A dictionary maps each command name to its function, so there's no long chain of
ifs.
And main is the single place that catches toolkit errors, printing one clean line
and returning one, instead of a traceback.
And dunder main is what runs when you type python dash m toolkit.
It calls main, and raises system exit with the return value, which becomes the
program's exit code.
Let's run the finished tool.
Help is generated by argparse, listing the three commands.
The sample file is fully valid.
The broken file reports four precise problems.
And the exit code is one, which is how other programs know validation failed.
The Markdown report.
Ten requests with an eighty percent success rate.
And notice the average latency, over four seconds.
That's because one failed request took thirty seconds.
An average hides outliers like that, which is why one of this module's challenges
asks you to add a percentile.
With format json and out, the report is saved to a file instead, and the folder is
created automatically.
Here's the start of that JSON file, ready for a dashboard or another program.
In strict mode, the broken file fails, with the warning on standard error.
And settings come from the environment.
Point the prices file at something that doesn't exist, and you get one clear error
line, no traceback.
Finally, fetch.
A local web server is serving the data folder on port eighty-seven sixty-five, just
like in lesson five.
To keep the command short, we store the base address in a shell variable.
Both files download concurrently, and fifteen records are merged into one file.
Validating the merged file finds the eleven good records and the same four problems.
And if a server can't be reached, again, one clear line explains what happened.
A demo shows that the tool works today.
Tests make sure it keeps working when you change it.
We use pytest.
A pytest test is just a function whose name starts with test, using plain assert
statements.
Good row is a fixture.
Pytest sees the parameter name and passes in a fresh valid dictionary, defined once
in conftest dot py.
Parametrize runs the same test once per value.
Here, five tests, each deleting a different required field, and checking that the
error names that field.
This one feeds in nine kinds of bad data, including the sneaky True posing as a
number, and checks each is rejected for the right field.
Tests must not depend on a real network, which could be slow or down. httpx's mock
transport replaces the network with a function that returns fake responses.
So we can check that two downloads are merged in the right order.
And that a four oh four, or a response that isn't a list, becomes a toolkit error.
These run in milliseconds, with no server at all.
Run the whole suite.
Forty-two tests, all passing, in a fraction of a second.
With dash v, pytest lists each test by name.
And mypy confirms that all our type hints are consistent.
First, running a file inside the package directly.
Python can't find the toolkit package, because it searches from the toolkit folder
itself.
The fix: stay in the project root and run python dash m toolkit.
Second, forgetting the virtual environment.
With the environment deactivated, the system Python doesn't have httpx installed.
The fix is to activate dot venv again.
Is not valid JSON usually means a trailing comma, single quotes, or a comment.
The message gives you the line and column.
File not found usually means you ran the command from another folder.
Relative paths start from where you run it.
On Windows, if PowerShell refuses to run the activate script, run Set Execution
Policy for the current user with Remote Signed, once.
And if text comes out garbled, make sure every read and write uses utf eight.
You used lists, dictionaries, and sets, and built conversations as lists of message
dictionaries.
You wrote functions, dataclasses, and your own exceptions.
You organised a package, and worked with files, JSON, and environment variables.
You added type hints, made HTTP requests, and ran downloads concurrently.
And you built a tested command line tool with clear errors and proper exit codes.
Module quiz, question one.
An agent may only use two tools.
Which structure gives the fastest check for whether a tool is allowed?
A set.
Membership checks on a set stay fast however large it grows.
Question two.
What does frozen equals True add to our usage record?
Fields can't be changed after the record is created.
And note, a dataclass does not validate types by itself.
That's why from dict checks every field.
Question three.
Which block runs every time, whether or not an error happens?
Finally.
That's why it's used for cleanup.
Question four.
Why does fetch all use asyncio dot gather?
To download everything concurrently, so the total time is roughly the slowest
download, not the sum of all of them.
And question five.
Where should the real API key for your project live?
In an environment variable, or a dot env file that git ignores.
The example file only ever holds fake placeholders.
If you want to go further, here's your extension challenge.
Pick one or more, and for each one, write the code and a test.
Add a top N option to the report command.
Add ninety-fifth percentile latency, which, unlike the average, isn't distorted by
one slow request.
Add a breakdown per day, using the created at timestamp.
Or add a CSV output format, with the standard csv module.
These are the official documentation pages for everything we used.
Links are in the description, and the full source code is in the course repository.
That's Module 1 complete.
You now have the Python foundation that the rest of this course is built on.
In Module 2, you'll finally talk to a language model: tokens, context windows,
message history, structured output, rate limits, and costs, and you'll build an AI
Study Assistant that explains concepts and generates quizzes.
See you there.
